name: Biosun 'Hopi' ear candles

card.summary: A branded hollow-cone ear candle marketed as 'Hopi' candles for ear-wax and general well-being care, a name the Hopi Tribal Council disputes.
card.note: Regulators including the FDA and Health Canada warn of burns and ear injury, and the Hopi Tribal Council says the practice is not Hopi.

quick.overview:
Biosun is a manufacturer that sold hollow ear candles under the name 'Hopi' ear candles. Users light the far end of the cone while the narrow end sits at the ear opening, and sellers describe the result as clearing wax and impurities, a grooming and ear-care routine some people add to a wellness regimen.

The branding has been controversial. The Hopi Tribal Council says ear candling was never part of Hopi tradition and asked Biosun to stop using the name; research on ear candling in general has not found wax removal, and regulators warn about burns.
quick.how: Practitioners and spa clients use the candle in a lying-down session at home or in a salon, with the lit cone held over the ear while a helper watches it burn. Marketing describes it as relaxing and cleansing. Product use is typically described as a short session per ear.
quick.risks: The FDA issued a 2007 alert citing burn and middle-ear damage risks, and Health Canada warned of injury especially to children. Reported complications include burns, wax blockage and eardrum perforation, and at least two house fires, one fatal, have been linked to ear candling. Both agencies restrict sales that carry medical claims.

lead: Biosun is a manufacturer whose hollow wax-and-fabric ear candles were sold as 'Hopi' ear candles. [1] Ear candling, also called ear coning, involves lighting one end of a hollow candle placed at the ear opening; proponents claim the heat creates suction that draws wax and impurities from the ear and benefits general health. [1]

The 'Hopi' name is disputed. The Hopi Tribal Council states that the practice has never been part of Hopi tradition and asked Biosun to stop using the name, which Biosun kept using for over a decade; the product was later rebranded 'traditional earcandles' in Germany, though some US resellers still say 'Hopi'. [1]

Studies of ear candling generally, including a 1996 Spokane ear, nose and throat clinic study, found no negative pressure and no wax removal, and the residue left in candles matches the residue from candles burned without an ear. [1] No study has tested this specific brand separately.

chain: Lit hollow cone placed at the ear opening
Sellers describe warmth drawing out wax and 'toxins'
Aim: clean ears and a relaxing grooming ritual
angle.text: People use the candles as an ear-cleaning and relaxation routine, with the aim of cleaner-feeling ears and a spa-style grooming session. The claimed wax removal has not been shown in published testing.

paras: The candle is a hollow cone or tube, typically cloth coated with wax, that is lit at the upper end while the narrow end is positioned at the ear canal opening. [1] Sellers describe the practice as ear cleansing and relaxation. [1]

No documented origin exists for ear candling; advocates have cited Chinese, Egyptian and North American roots and even Atlantis, while the earliest records suggest practice by Americans in the 20th century, largely in Arizona, after European immigrants introduced it. [1]

The Hopi Tribal Council has said the practice was never part of Hopi tradition and asked Biosun to drop the name. Biosun kept using it for more than a decade before the product was rebranded in Germany. [1]

A 1996 study at a Spokane ear, nose and throat clinic found no negative pressure and no wax removal; residue collected after candling matched residue from burned candles not placed in an ear, namely wax and soot. [1] Edzard Ernst has concluded there are no data showing effectiveness for any condition. [1]

The FDA issued a 2007 alert citing risks of burns and middle-ear damage, and Health Canada found no health benefit and warned of injury risk, especially to children. Both agencies restrict sales that carry medical claims. [1]

Reported complications include burns (the most common, per a survey of ear, nose and throat surgeons), wax blockage and eardrum perforation, and at least two house fires, one fatal, have been linked to ear candling accidents. [1]
No studies found. Studies of ear candling in general, not of this brand, are described above. [1]

timeline.event: Spokane ENT clinic study finds no wax removal from ear candling. [1]
